summary: Children aged 6–7 add and subtract a two-digit number and ones by bridging through a multiple of ten: partition the ones to land on the decade, then add or subtract the remainder (36 + 7 → 36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 4 → 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48). Core activities use a manipulable number line and base-ten blocks — with ten-frames and a hundred square as alternative views — so the new ten is seen forming and the tens digit updates for a visible reason, with mixed bridging and non-bridging items (43 + 5) so children decide when a boundary is actually crossed. Fluency practice, a static anchor image, and a narrate-your-method conversation are retained as complementary approaches with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: Adding the ones digits and ignoring the new ten (36 + 7 → 33 or '313').
Counting on/back in ones and slipping by one at the tens boundary.
Failing to change the tens digit when the ones cross a multiple of ten.
Bridging when it isn't needed, or not bridging when it is.
For subtraction, stopping at the decade (52 − 4 → 50) or miscounting past it.

activities.title: Bridge the decade on a number line with a base-ten mat
steps: Work 36 + 7 by first jumping from 36 to the next decade (40), then completing the jump with the remaining ones (to 43).
On a base-ten mat, watch four loose ones combine with the existing ones to make a whole new ten-stick as the jump reaches 40, so the tens digit change has a visible cause.
Switch to subtraction mode for 52 − 4: jump back to the decade first (52 − 2 = 50), then take the remaining 2 to reach 48.
Mix in non-bridging items such as 43 + 5 and decide for each item whether the ones cross a decade before choosing to bridge.

Optionally view the same bridging in another representation: a ten-frame filling up to a complete ten of ones, or a hundred square where you move along a row and drop to the next row as you cross the decade, so the new ten is seen forming in more than one way.
State out loud which decade you bridge through and why the tens digit does or does not change.
activities.insight: When adding makes the ones fill up to a whole ten, a new ten is formed and the tens digit increases by one; when subtracting takes away more ones than there are, a ten is broken into ones and the tens digit decreases by one (52 − 4 = 48). Partitioning the ones to reach the decade makes this regrouping explicit for both addition and subtraction.

activities.title: Fluency practice: fill in, draw the jump, choose the decade
steps: Complete fill-in results such as 36 + 7 = ___ mentally or with a jotting.
Draw the two-part bridging jump on an empty number line to show reaching the decade and then continuing.
Choose which decade you bridge through for a given calculation, with decade options as the choices (for 36 + 7 the decade is 40).
In a separate results question, identify the correct total, where a distractor such as 33 for 36 + 7 reflects the ignore-the-new-ten error (keeping the original tens digit).
Include at least one non-bridging item so you practise recognising when no bridge is needed.
activities.insight: Once the bridging strategy is understood, spaced and varied practice builds fluency in partitioning the ones and updating the tens digit accurately.

activities.title: Anchor image: a worked bridging number line
steps: Study a number line showing 36 → 40 → 43 with the regrouped ten labelled, revealing each step in turn.
Describe in your own words why the jump stops at 40 before continuing to 43.
activities.insight: A clear worked picture shows what a bridging jump looks like and names the new ten, giving a reference model for the two-part method.

activities.title: Narrate your method: how did you get across the ten?
steps: Work a bridging item and a non-bridging item, then explain aloud how you got across the ten (or why you did not need to).
Answer questions such as 'Why does the tens digit change here?' and 'For 43 + 5, did you need to cross a ten? How do you know?'
Show 52 − 4 on the number line and say where you stopped on the way.
activities.insight: Articulating the decade step and the reason the tens digit changes reveals whether the child is partitioning to bridge or merely counting in ones.

checkQuestion: Work these out — mentally or on the number line — and talk me through each: 36 + 7; 52 − 4; 43 + 5.
checkAnswer: 43; 48; 48. Watch for bridging through the decade on the first two (36 + 4 = 40, + 3 = 43; 52 − 2 = 50, − 2 = 48) and a straightforward ones-addition on the third, which does not cross a ten.
